Ho Lun Chan1,2 , Elena Romanovskaia1,2, Sean H. Mills3,4, Valentin Romanovski1,2, Xikai Wang1,2, Iliana Marrujo3, Harjot Singh1,2, Andrew M. Minor3,4, Peter Hosemann5,6 & John R. Scully1,2

The corrosion dealloying behavior of cold-worked (CW) Ni20Cr alloy (wt%) was studied in molten LiF- NaF-KF (or FLiNaK) salts at 600 °C, equal to a homologous temperature (TH) of 0.52. Alloys were coldrolled to achieve reductions of thickness of 10%, 30%, and 50% introducing plastic deformation and a high density of dislocations. Potentiostatic holds (Eapplied) were applied in two different electrode potential regimes. At 1.75VKþ=K, Cr dealloying to Cr(II) and Cr(III) is predominant, while at 1.90 VKþ=K, both Ni and Cr are oxidized in molten FLiNaK at 600 °C. In these potential regimes, dealloyed Ni20Cr displayed bicontinuous porosity within the grain interior and at grain boundaries, driven by the high driving force for Cr dissolution and sustained by defect mediated outward solid state diffusion of Cr in parallel with surface diffusion of Ni. The bicontinuous porous structure developed was observed to undergo further coarsening and densiﬁcation of the Ni-rich ligaments at a higher electrode potential. The main effect of CW observed is the introduction of plastic deformation and dislocation substructures that serve as short-circuit paths for Cr solid state diffusion to surfaces exposed to FLiNaK. This modiﬁed the evolution of the bicontinuous porous structure which increased with CW substantially. Kinetic analysis reveals that the Cr dealloying at +1.75 VKþ=K and 1.90 VKþ=K is initially charge transfer controlled, except for the 50% CW condition at 1.90 VKþ=K, where the process becomes limited by slow Cr defect mediated bulk diffusion. The rate determining factors are explored and compared to experimental results.

A critical milestone toward deploying molten salt reactor technology is ensuring the durability of structural alloys used for reactor vessels and heatexchanging loops1–5. Alloys considered for use in MSR and other salt systems are exposed to an array of harsh environments, such as hightemperature molten salts, corrosion due to thermal gradients coupled with impurities functioning as oxidants, radiation, and stress, posing critical challenges even to nuclear reactor alloys speciﬁed in the ASME Section III division 5, such as Alloy 800H, Alloy 617, and stainless steel 316H6. Among these challenges, the understanding of corrosion and its associated degradation mechanism is crucial for predicting the operational lifespan and thus has been the subject of intensiﬁed laboratory research in recent years7–12. It is widely reported that intergranular corrosion (IGC) is a predominant form of corrosion attack observed across several alloy systems in

molten chlorides and ﬂuorides7,9,13,14. While the normally protective oxides of structural alloys are unstable under these conditions13, alloying elements thatarethermodynamicallylessnoble(LN),e.g.,CrandFeinNi-containing alloys, will be selectively “dealloyed” owing to their high thermodynamic driving force for spontaneous dissolution at commonly observed corrosion potentials with an oxidant and easy solubilization of their metal cations. Dealloying is also aided by Cr availability from the bulk supplied to the outward surface via short-circuit diffusion pathways, e.g., grain boundaries (GBs)14,15 and dislocation networks. Which of these elements will be selectivelyremoveddependsonthepreciseelectrodepotentialsensedbythealloy relative to the thermodynamic equilibrium of their oxidized species, e.g., Cr(III), Ni(II), relative to the elemental state (i.e., Cr), unique to each salt chemistry16,17. Although this phenomena is not well investigated for molten salt systems, it has recently been observed on Ni20Cr (wt%), Fe-Cr-Ni, and Fe-Ni alloys in molten chloride salts between 500 oC and 800 oC20–24,26, and may increase the susceptibility to stress corrosion cracking (SCC)27–30 or transition to creep induced cracking31–33. In our recent work, model Ni20Cr (wt%) alloys were subjected to applied potentials in molten LiF-NaF-KF (FLiNaK) at 600 oC between 1.75 and 2.75 VKþ=K

34. A potentiostatic hold (i.e., applied potential) was selected to impose a controlled constant potential driving force for Cr dealloying, such that the corrosion process does not entirely rely on oxidizing salt impurities, which are inherently difﬁcult to control. Between +1.75, +1.90, and +2.10 VKþ=K, bicontinuous porosity with remaining µm-scale surface MN ligaments and dealloying depth was observed. These features are attributed to MN element surface diffusion, metal/salt interfacial LN dissolution, and LN element defect-mediated bulk outward diffusion, occurring simultaneously25–27,35. At high homologous temperatures (TH = 0.4–0.6),theeffectofLNelementbulkdiffusionisparticularlynotable during molten salt corrosion (TH = 0.4–0.6)25–27,35; the rate of MN element surface diffusion dictates the interfacial morphological evolution and has been shown to form µm-scale ligaments, similarly in the case of liquid metal dealloying36–38. This situation raises a new question: when the rate and mechanism of LN element outward defect mediated bulk diffusion are altered, how would the rate and morphology of dealloying be affected? Answering this question is especially crucial for MSR alloy development since factors including irradiation39, stress induced by thermal gradients40, thermomechanical processing41–45, and its residual stress8,46, are known to form non-equilibrium point and line defects and dislocation substructures, such as low angle grain boundaries, deformation twins, nonequilibrium vacancies, and even new phases, that operate in parallel with bulk diffusion in a perfect lattice with only near-equilibrium vacancies. It is well established that plastic deformation in face-centered cubic (FCC) structured metal alloys is controlled by their stacking fault energy (SFE)47. Ni-based alloys have a relatively high SFE47 and reduced SF widths, inﬂuencing their mechanical properties, such as promoting cross-slip and reducingthelikelihoodof deformationtwinning.Theresultingdeformation structurestypicallyexhibitdislocationwallsormicrobands48,49.Forinstance, transmission electron microscopy studies48,49 show that cold-worked (CW) Ni-Cr alloy may exhibit planar dislocation pileup and densiﬁcation into low-angle GBs on stacking faults at a low degree of CW (5%). Interconnected dislocation cell (DC) structures were observed at a moderate degree of CW (10–30%), eventually forming microbands at a high degree of CW (>50%)45,50. These characteristics of severe plastic deformation are also observed by Dudova et al.50 and Koukolikova et al.45. In prior studies, CW has been shown to increase the susceptibility of austenitic stainless steels51, 316L44,52, and alloy 69053–55 to SCC in simulated pressurized water reactor environments. In molten Li2CO3-K2CO3- Na2CO3 at450 °C,cold workingimpedes theabilityofInconel601to forma uniform protective oxide ﬁlm, which appears to demonstrate more adherence to highly strained lattice areas and dislocation end points56. According to ref. 44, a high degree of CW (50%) on 316SS has led to subgrains characterized by the densiﬁcation of high geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) and high-angle GBs. These observations correlate with signiﬁcant intergranular dealloying and possible bicontinuous dealloying within the grain interior in molten FLiNaK, 700 °C. A similar observation was made pertaining 316LSS alloys in molten FLiNaK, 600 °C57. Therefore, there is a notional observation that susceptibility to bicontinuous dealloying and the depth of dealloying attack in moltensalts may be increased by 1- and 2-dimensional defects induced by CW. In our prior work34,thepossiblediffusionthatcontrolsthemoltensaltdealloyingprocess was identiﬁed by calculating and comparing the ﬂux for Cr interfacial oxidation to Cr(III) (i.e., Jelectric) to the Cr defect mediated bulk outward

This comparison helps to inform whether Cr bulk diffusion is sufﬁciently rapid to support Cr oxidation at an applied potential in the susceptibility range. In the case of a Ni20Cr (wt%) alloy with minimal CW, Jbulk was found to be rate-controlling in molten FLiNaK at 600 °C34. A similar approach was also employed in this work toelucidate the role of CW on dealloying particularly, to support the hypothesis that CW can increase Jbulk due to the introduction of deformation induced high dislocation densities50. This work studied the potentiostatic dealloying behavior of 10%, 30%, and50%CWNi20Cr(wt%)alloyinmoltenFLiNaKsaltsat600 °C.Thegoal was to understand how CW alters the corrosion rate-determining step or steps of dealloying as a function of plastic deformation. The method for potentiostatic dealloying is based on our prior work34 in which +1.75 VKþ=K and +1.90 VKþ=K were applied to the test alloys for 10 ks. A multi-modal suite of characterization methods, including electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), were utilized to characterize morphology, dealloying depth and velocity to understand how the material’s grain orientation, microstructure, dislocation substructure developed during cold working affected dealloying. Moreover, the rate of dealloying and possible rate limiting steps were discussed. For instance, the ﬂux of Cr to the metal/ salt interface by defect mediated outward diffusion, charge transfer controlled reaction rate at the metal/salt interface and lastly the mass transport controlledﬂuxofCr(II)andCr(III)inthesaltawayfrommetal/saltinterface all occur in series and were compared to each other to gain insights on the controlling phenomena.

Methods Materials preparation Ni20Cr alloys (80 wt%Ni-20 wt%Cr) were fabricated by a vacuum arcmelting process in this study. Ni slugs (99.98%, Thermo Scientiﬁc) and Cr pieces (99.99%, Thermo Scientiﬁc) were ﬁrst mixed at the targeted weight ratio, melted, and remelted at least three times under a high vacuum environment of >10−5 torr. The as-cast alloys were then encapsulated in an Ar-ﬁlled quartz tube and solutionized at 1050 °C for 6 h, followed by water quenching at room temperature. Using this process, the as-homogenized alloys demonstrated a uniform composition, characterized by a single FCC phase and a grain size of >100 μm58. The alloys were then machined into rectangular plates with the dimensions of 20 ± 0.2 × 1 ± 0.2 × 1 ± 0.2 mm, polished to a 1200-grit surface ﬁnish using silicon carbide paper. CW was achieved by cold rolling to reduce cross-sectional area by 10%, 30%, and 50%,quantiﬁedusingthechange in cross-sectional area ((A0–Af)/A0·100%). The tests were conducted in the as-rolled conditions without further heat treatment. Lastly, the as-homogenized alloys are referred to as “0% CW”.

The calculation of these diffusion ﬂuxes was considered in one dimension. Ni surface diffusion is recognized but not directly considered.
